comments.author: @paullukaszewicz2165
comments.text:
Hi Wes, I have watched probably a couple dozen of your videos at this point, usually anonymously. I think that you in particular come at this subject the most clear eyed and unbiased. There is near zero hype in your coverage. I appreciate your work on this subject. As a side note, I also enjoy your subtle puns. What I am about to write will be lengthy, and I get that most people won't want to read it in its entirety. So, I will include a synopsis. 

TL;DR:
We cannot expect the government to solve our problems with AI. They are currently captured by capital and business interests. Even if they weren't captured, they would be too slow to regulate in a timely manner given how quickly AI will develop. Capital will never willingly give away power, control, and ownership. Economics rarely behave the way textbooks and economists would have you believe. Economics are like some old gods we created with fanciful stories that are supposed to explain how things work. The letter that was written by Sam Altman and his co-authors ignore these real problems. 

Also, a critical mistake the authors make, is believing that prices falling is a good thing. It is not. Most of the common people of the world are in some sort of debt, e.g. mortgages, student loans, credit cards, auto loans, et cetera. How can anyone repay these debts without income and with massive deflation? They cannot, and will be forced to own nothing. Do not expect Universal Basic Income to arrive on time, if ever. Humans have not evolved past cruelty in a mere 100-200 years. Expect a thirst for power and dominance unrivaled by the kingdoms of the past. Especially with autonomous soldiers at their disposal with no accountability. We are at a critical juncture, but to portray capitalism as the way forward, is near extinction level folly. 
:END TL;DR

There are some things I wanted to get out of the way first. Why should you care what I think? Well, I have degrees in Finance and Information Technology. These are topics I have studied and are familiar with. In the past I have also lived in Silicon Valley and worked for investment firms. Back in 2017, people looked at me like I was an alien when I started talking about AI. Back then I was reading books by authors like: Ray Kurzweil, Max Tegmark, Nick Bostrom and Kai-Fu Lee. Their ideas and the implications of AI have been marinating in my grey matter for some time. I had even considered writing a book on the subject. Am I the penultimate authority on one particular subject matter? No. But, I see the more complete picture and very pragmatically. 

Most AI researchers tend to be thoughtful, good natured, and compassionate people. That is why their predictions tend to skew more positively. This is especially true for those that are extreme specialists. They see humanity progressing everyday and are very insulated from the dismal domain of regular people. We should not misinterpret their bias as to what reality will become. The same is true for capitalists. In their minds, the world of economics, financialization, pricing and labor are all natural facts of man. Never invented by man, but some how passed down on us from the divine. Immutable laws as it were.

Modern economics is fundamentally flawed. Two of its major suppositions are laughable. Firstly, consumers and producers are rational. If you have ever met a human, you know this to be false. Especially if life and death are on the line, or Tickle Me Elmo… Second, is that infinite growth is possible. It is not. The Earth has finite mass and resources. This means that competition is not guaranteed. This then means that prices following free market theories are, also, not guaranteed. It is our duty to see resources rationally allocated in order to minimize human suffering, not ensure mega yachts for the most morally bankrupt among us.

There is a reason why the Federal Reserve consistently has 2% inflation as its target. A slight inflation has the benefit of price stability, therefore consumers and producers can better predict expenditures. Too high of inflation and capital’s ability to predict markets based on return becomes difficult. Too much deflation, means that consumers in debt have a much heavier burden to pay back stifling demand (which is the basis of modern economies), and incentivizing capital to save for a return, rather than invest. 

Look at Japan’s deflationary economy and their problems. So, to have some gigantic deflationary event that pushes prices to the floor, while regular people have debt up to their eyeballs after years of easy credit, will be devastating. Imagine having to pay off a $300,000 mortgage with no income and now in real terms that $300,000 is more like $30,000,000. Yea, no thanks. Bankruptcy for everyone, yay! (Unless you have student loans then you’d better pray). 

Some may argue that it is now up to those in government to regulate and legislate these problems with AI. They will not in their current state. Almost all sovereign governments have become mills pumping out crony capitalism. Playing favorites with whomever bribes their campaigns the most and completely ignoring the will of the people. Why? Because some super small group of people in fancy robes were really good at not getting caught taking their bribes first. We cannot take our governments seriously enough to function as intended, let alone behave with extraordinary expedience and clarity. Even if they were functioning normally, I doubt their response would be rapid enough to blunt the worst of the economic disaster that is about to unfold.

In the minds of many, but especially in the United States, Universal Basic Income, or any other social program, will be met with skepticism and disdain. Mind rot of “oh no that’s commie stuff, we ain’t gonna let that happen in merica” will surely be rampant. This hesitancy from the pre-programmed rugged individualists will tell everyone to pull themselves up by their bootstraps even if they don’t have shoes on their feet. What’s worse, is that the corporate media goons will feed this idea, even on the “left.”

I get the sense from the loudest voices in the broad, meta-discussion that everything is more likely to turn out roses, rather than dystopian nightmare. Personally, I could not feel more opposite. As the world stands now, we are predisposed to follow the bad track towards dystopia at best and obliteration at worst. It is for the reasons mentioned above that I say this. If we as a people do not circumvent power structures that will be roadblocks and make real moves toward solving our own problems, humanity is lost to the worst among us.

While I could probably write a whole book or thesis on this topic, I’m sure like 2 people will read this entire thing in a YouTube comment section. So, I will end it here with one last bit. Having lived in the Bay Area and feeling some of the animosity towards technologists, those people that lit that Waymo car on fire aren’t some anti-progress luddites. The normal people of Silicon Valley are tired of their cities being turned into playthings and testing grounds for ultra rich tech bros who seemingly don’t care about anyone but themselves. They are tired of their needs being ignored and outsiders with stacks of cash being treated with white gloves. They are tired of working crap jobs, to barely tread water, while someone treats their city and home like an experiment. Most of all, they are tired of being the ones feeling the negative outcomes of some supposed public good, only to never gain from that good.     

P.S. Martin Shkreli totally meant what he wrote and probably thought he was cool for doing so.

The regular response of "adapt or be left behind." is hard to grasp when the very thing we need to survive is being automated away. What does one "adapt" to when a.i can adapt faster and cheaper? 

This is a multi-faceted issue. People are wondering how they're going to eat and pay rent. People have a bitter feeling of corporations and business practices around technology. This is not an "I hate progress/tech!" fear but a "How am I going to take care of my family??" one. The latter question is not the problem of corporations but politicians and governments. The industrial revolution saw farmers become factory workers and a lot of fears came with that. But, along that came worker protections, paid time off, 40-hour max hours, etc.

We developed an operating system on top of the new paradigm to operate the exchange of labor in a balanced way so production can take place without killing workers. 
What's happening is there's no foreseeable new operating system for this new "post labor" paradigm a.I is about to unleash on us and people are rightfully terrified. What's the worker protections in this new revolution? How does health insurance work? Will a.i companies advertise to me all the time? Again, problems solved by governments.

The anger should be focused on the government to wake up and start creating the new O.S to manage this new revolution. All "regular" people see is more corporations taking more data and releasing more products that do nothing. All people want is to finally be included in the new paradigm in a fair way because why should people be excited that a.i and robots drive housing down 80% if the rent still increases? 27:03 "regular" people hear that and go yeah right. The bottleneck in progress is the social and political solutions, two things Altman himself said is a harder problem to solve than AGI. I see a.i companies saying we're the ones not ready. No, people aren't ready for corporations to corporate. That sentiment fuels the fear.


Universal Basic Income. Rent protections. Government work programs. Who's making progress in these areas with the same energy as OpenAI chasing agi? NOBODY. So yeah, I'd be scared too.

Echoing what folks have already wrote here and what you mention in the video as well, the driver of capital is profit which leads to shareholder value.    Without some regulations around the use of AI and taxing any cost savings when displacing human jobs, companies will continue to enrich their bottomline.   

So rather than the simplistic 2.5% of company valuation annually, which seems ridiculously low to me, we should be coming up with some formula around what amount of AI usage is equivalent to manpower and then take a sizeable chunk out those cost savings and tax those heavily. 

So for instance, if I employ AI to replace my personal assistant and say they were paid 100k/y.  If AI can do that job for 5k/y, I've saved $95k/y and should be happy paying say 50% of those savings to the people who lost that job in the form of UBI.

I get the whole "over time everything will be cheaper" idea, but before that curve accelerates, job loss will make everyone much less able to afford ANYTHING.  So we need to treat this as like digital layoffs and the people who are replaced should have a substantial safety net paid for by these employers.

It seems hard to believe that billions are being spent on AI to create systems that autonomously do what "they" want. Our tech leaders are shrewd business people. It would seem that billions are being spent because AI does what the tech leaders want and returns many more billions in value to their operations. Just saying.

Being a user of AI, I find it an amazing revolutionary technology. AI is a bulldozer for unstructured digital information (documents, audio, video, social media posts, etc). There was a time when ditches were dug by hand using men with shovels and animals. Then along came the game changing backhoe. Likewise a person using AI can craft written works, images, and videos in short order that would take an enormous amount of time or require a big team to accomplish. 


AI is an aggregator of the information it was trained on. It does not create anything new. It effectively disassembles it's training data and then reassembles it in a new way under the direction of a human.  It is an extremely clever mechanism but is always using those "Lego bricks" found in the training data. Lego bricks have their limitations. When you sign up for ChatGPT, for example, you are warned that the AI can give out wrong answers. Not that it tells lies, but if the training data was wrong then the results will be wrong. As with all computer systems garbage in => garbage out.  

While I do think AI is a completely amazing set of tools that will propel productivity into a new era, I do not believe that it will ever be sentient or fully autonomous. Furthermore it seems to me that the AI industry pushes this idea (the singularity) as well as the idea that AI is smarter than humans. This looks like juiced up marketing. The software industry is famous for selling "vapor-ware". That is products that don't exist but can reasonably be expected to be delivered in a given amount of time with given resources. Many times in the past these products were complete failures as the underlying assumptions of what could be done by when turned out to be wrong. These stories about sentient AI are always peppered with words like "could" or "may" and are IMHO just hype to fill up the sales queue.

There is a magician like quality to AI hype. A recent video of puppies playing in the snow looks flawless. But was that the first rendition? We will never know - but I doubt it. How many times was the "prompt" adjusted by a human to get that result? We don't know as the magician is not telling. But in my experience generative image AI produces results with the occasional six fingered person with three legs. While human supervision is required the productivity increase is still amazing. 

For artists that fear their jobs will be taken away - the answer is likely yes. But humans with an artistic eye are needed to supervise generative AI output. So it's a matter of repackaging one's skills to for the new paradigm. Painting using an easel and brushes is going away. But the underlying skill of an "artist's perspective" is not. Likewise the demand for men with shovels to dig ditches  is gone - but the need to understand where to put the ditch is not.

What is going to happen to the displaced? No one knows. There is some vague talk about UBI (Universal Basic Income). But no details. It's something that needs to be brought into the forefront and planed for in a serious credible way.  


AI is not going to take your job. But somebody using an AI will. Likewise AI will not take over the world but somebody using AI could - if humanity believes in this AGI mythology and submits. Recall the Wizard of Oz. When the curtain was pulled on the fire breathing dragon there was a human at the controls.

comments.text: I think Sam Altman's opinion on the future is incorrect.  First, the value of labor will never reach perfect zero.  Real-world constraints will apply to AI as much as it does to humans: things like space, time, difficulty of manipulating things, etc.  A robot delivery driver will still need to drive and deliver things.  You cannot make that process infinitely efficient, and a human would be able to do it at least half as well as a robot, so whatever value a delivery will have, a human will be able to trade their labor for at least half of that.  In addition, taxing capital and redistributing to those with less, while labor has a value of near zero, would effectively destroy humans.  You're effectively sending out the economic signal to humans that nothing they do matters, but they get free stuff. That will end exactly like the mouse utopia experiment.  Don't get me wrong, there's definitely a level of "too much struggle" for humans that becomes demoralizing.  But "too little struggle" is even worse--it will breed a culture that leads to self-destruction.  Moreover, labor does not exist in a vacuum.  Labor and demand drive each other.  For instance, the number of dentists is proportional to the number of people that exist, just like the number of farmers is proportional to the number of people that need to eat. So the number of robots will be balanced by the number of humans and robots that each robot requires in order to live, just like the number of humans will be balanced by the number of humans and robots they rely on to live.  So, the number of things produced will reach an equilibrium with the number of things consumed.  In other words, the price of cars will never reach zero, because there will never be an infinite surplus of cars while demand remains constant.  So the idea of "things getting twice as cheap every few years" is a fallacy on its own.  Cars may become a little bit cheaper, if its possible to make the production of cars more efficient.  However, infinite efficiency is not possible, and marginal value will still be the name of the game.  No robot would produce a trillion cars just so they can sell them for $0.01.  That would be stupid and wasteful of resources that could be used to produce other goods that would yield higher profits.  I think a much darker reality is that with hyper-intelligent AI, humans will quickly become nothing more than pets.  Robots that are smarter than humans will out-compete, out-negotiate, out-plan, and generally outwit us.  Increasingly, humans won't matter, because all high society, intellectual discourse, publications, and complex theory will be dominated by AI.  The smartest among us would be like a low-IQ child capable only of mild annoyance to an AI being.  The AI/robots would naturally end up with all important capital (land, natural resources, machinery, etc), and they'll achieve that non-violently simply by shrewd trading, planning, and self-control.  In time, they'll probably take what they can from this planet and leave to colonize another, leaving us with a desolate wasteland ravaged by climate instability and depleted natural resources.
